sermon:
## A Gospel That Grows in the Dark
*The word of truth bears fruit before anyone is watching*

**Text:** Colossians 1:1-14 · **Supporting:** Mark 4:28 · Philippians 1:6 · Ephesians 4:1 · Isaiah 55:11

Paul never met them. The church at Colossae was not his work and not his church, a congregation in a fading town off the main road, planted while he sat chained in a room he could not leave. And the first thing he does is give thanks. Not for results he engineered. Not for a movement he could put his name on. For fruit he never planted, growing in soil he never walked.

**The fruit was already growing before they noticed it**
Watch the verbs, because the verbs preach the sermon. "Of which you heard before in the word of the truth of the gospel; which is come unto you, as it is in all the world; and bringeth forth fruit, as it doth also in you, since the day ye heard it, and knew the grace of God in truth" (Colossians 1:5-6). The gospel is doing the growing. Not the Colossians. Not even Epaphras, the man who carried it to them and prayed it into them. The word itself, planted in a person, bears fruit the way seed does — quietly, on its own clock, without the farmer understanding the mechanism. Jesus said it plainly: "For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear" (Mark 4:28). Of herself. The Greek there is automatē — automatically, without visible cause, the seed working underground while the man who scattered it sleeps and rises and has no idea how. We want a method. We want a strategy we can teach at a conference and replicate on a chart. Scripture gives us soil and seed and a God who makes things live underground where no camera reaches. Isaiah heard the same promise from the far end of the covenant: "so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please" (Isaiah 55:11). The word does not come back empty. It comes back carrying fruit. That is not a sentiment to hang on a wall. It is closer to a physics — a law about how God's word behaves in the world He made. And it has been doing this since the day it landed, "since the day ye heard it," Paul says, not since the day you got serious, not since the day you finally figured out the technique. From the first hearing the seed was already at work.

**Paul prays for the wrong thing on purpose**
Now read what he actually asks God to give them, because it will expose what you have been asking God for yourself. He does not pray they would be comfortable. He does not pray they would be safe, or successful, or spared the hard year. "That ye might be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; that ye might walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work" (Colossians 1:9-10). Knowledge that produces a walk. Understanding that changes how a person spends a Tuesday afternoon when no one religious is watching. To walk worthy — Paul uses the same word to the Ephesians, "walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called" (Ephesians 4:1) — is not to earn the calling but to carry it the way a man carries a name he was given and did not deserve. And the fruit of that walk is not applause, and it is not ease. It is endurance. "Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness" (Colossians 1:11). Read that again slowly. He prays they would be strong enough to wait. Strong enough to suffer without going bitter. Strong enough to stay joyful while the answer is delayed. That is the prayer of a man who knows exactly what the Christian life costs, and he is praying it from a cell, with a guard at the door, asking nothing for his own comfort and everything for theirs.

**You have been praying for the harvest and skipping the seed**
I have stood in my own pulpit and measured a year by what I could count — the attendance, the budget, the visible momentum — and the things I could count were never the things God was actually growing. We do this. We want the fruit visible and the growth fast and the proof in our hands, and we baptize our impatience and call it faith. But the gospel that came to Colossae was already bearing fruit before Paul wrote a single word, in people he would never meet, through a man whose name most Christians today could not tell you. The growth was real precisely because it did not depend on the man. And here is what lies under the whole prayer, the thing the entire rest of this letter exists to say out loud: the One who delivers us "from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son" (Colossians 1:13) is the same One who makes the seed grow. The gospel is not a program we run. It is a Person we receive, and a Person does the growing. So Paul can sit in chains and be confident "that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6). Not you. He. The work is His, the fruit is His, the kingdom is His Son's, and the redemption underneath all of it — "in whom we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins" (Colossians 1:14) — was bought and finished before you ever knew you needed it. So the question is not whether you are growing fast enough to satisfy yourself. The question is whether the seed is in the ground. Because if it is, He is at work in the dark, and the harvest was never on you.

The gospel grows where it lands.

## The One Who Holds the Pieces Together
*Christ is supreme over a creation that will not hold itself*

**Text:** Colossians 1:15-23 · **Supporting:** John 1:3 · Hebrews 1:3 · Romans 5:10 · Philippians 2:8

Everything is coming apart. You feel it in your body before you can put a word to it — the marriage fraying at an edge you cannot find, the country splitting along a seam you cannot stitch, the cells in your own frame turning against you on a schedule no one consulted you about. Entropy is not a mood you can pray away. It is the law the whole universe runs on, the slow unmaking written into matter itself. And into that law Paul drops a sentence that should stop the room.

**He is before all things, and He made all things**
"Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: for by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him" (Colossians 1:15-16). Image — eikōn — not a copy of God but the visible expression of the invisible One, God made seeable, the unseen rendered in a face you could look at. Firstborn — prōtotokos — and here the false teachers wanted to slip Christ into the ranks of creation, one more being among the powers. Paul slams that door. Firstborn is not first created. It is first in rank, the heir who owns the whole estate. John said the same thing from the other side: "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:3). Every thing. Not most things. Every thing. The thrones and the dominions, the very powers the Colossians were tempted to fear and flatter and appease — Paul lists them only to drag them out and set them under the feet of Christ. They did not make Him. He made them. And they exist for Him, which means the unseen forces a frightened person tries to bargain with at midnight already belong to the One that person is running from.

**He is before it, and right now He is holding it**
Then the line this whole letter is named for, and it is the most load-bearing sentence in the New Testament about why anything exists at all. "And he is before all things, and by him all things consist" (Colossians 1:17). Consist — sunestēken — they hold together, they cohere, they are kept from flying apart. The same testimony runs through Hebrews: He is "upholding all things by the word of his power" (Hebrews 1:3). This is not a watchmaker who wound the universe at the start and walked away to let it tick. This is a Sustainer whose active, present will is the only reason the atom does not unbind in this exact second. The reason your heart beat just now is not a closed mechanical system humming along on its own borrowed momentum. It is a Person holding the pieces in His hand and refusing to let go. Take away that hand and there is no slow decline, no gentle winding down. There is nothing. The cohesion of everything that exists — the binding of the atom, the orbit of the planet, the next beat of your pulse — is not a property of matter. It is a mercy of Christ, renewed every instant, that you have never once thanked Him for. He is before all things, so He depends on nothing to exist. And by Him all things consist, so everything depends on Him to exist at all. Take both clauses seriously and the universe stops being a machine and becomes a thing held, moment by moment, by a will that could let go in any given second and simply, mercifully, does not.

**And He held the worst piece of all — you**
Here is where it has to turn onto us, because the same hand that holds the galaxies reached down for the one part of creation that had set itself against Him. Paul did not flatter the Colossians and he will not flatter us. "And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled" (Colossians 1:21-22). Read the indictment before you reach for the comfort. Not estranged. Not distant. Not merely confused. Enemies — and enemies in the mind, which is to say at the level of the will, on purpose, with intent. I have been exactly that. I argued against God for a living, hostile to a God I claimed not even to believe in, which is its own quiet confession, because you do not fight that hard against something you are sure is not there. And the reconciliation came entirely from His side, not ours. "And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself" (Colossians 1:20). The One who holds all things together let Himself be torn apart. The Sustainer became the sacrifice. He "humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Philippians 2:8). And lest you think He waited for us to soften first, Paul tells Rome the timing: "when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). While we were still swinging. The hand that keeps the universe from collapsing is the same hand they drove a nail through. He did not hold the world together from a safe and sovereign distance. He held it together by coming apart on a Roman cross, at the precise moment we were doing our worst. So everything you are afraid is falling apart tonight — the family, the health, the faith, the whole fragile arrangement you cannot control — He is holding. Including you. Especially you.

In Him all things hold together.

## The Mystery Has a Name
*The secret hidden for ages is Christ in you*

**Text:** Colossians 1:24-2:5 · **Supporting:** Ephesians 3:5 · Galatians 2:20 · 1 Corinthians 1:24 · John 14:23

Every age goes looking for the hidden thing. The secret knowledge the masses do not have, the key behind the curtain, the inner circle that finally understands what the crowd never will. The Colossians had teachers promising exactly that — a deeper wisdom for the initiated, a higher tier past the basic gospel they got at the start, angels and visions and a knowing the ordinary believer had not yet climbed to. Paul has a mystery too. He uses the word freely. But he is about to do the one thing no peddler of secrets ever does. He is going to tell you what it is, out loud, in the open, to everyone.

**He suffers to make the secret public**
"Who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body's sake, which is the church" (Colossians 1:24). Read that carefully, because it is easy to wreck. Paul does not mean the cross was somehow short, that Christ's suffering left a gap his own pain has to fill — he just spent a paragraph saying that cross reconciled all things in heaven and earth. He means the suffering that comes from carrying the finished gospel into a hostile world still has to be borne by somebody, in real flesh, in real chains. And he volunteers. He counts the cost worth it because of what is being carried. The mystery is not protected by secrecy and sold at a price. It is published at cost and given away. "Even the mystery which hath been hid from ages and from generations, but now is made manifest to his saints" (Colossians 1:26). Made manifest — phaneroō, dragged into the daylight, the exact opposite of the hidden esoteric thing the false teachers were marketing. To the Ephesians he says the same of it: in other ages it was "not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit" (Ephesians 3:5). The secret of the universe was kept under seal for centuries and then thrown wide open to fishermen and slaves and Gentile housewives in a backwater town. That is not how secrets behave. That is how grace behaves.

**The mystery is not a what. It is a who.**
Then the sentence the whole struggle has been driving toward, and you could miss it because it is so short. "To whom God would make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles; which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). There it is. Not a doctrine to master. Not a technique to acquire. Not a tier to ascend to. A Person, indwelling. Christ in you. The most exalted being in existence, the One in whom all things hold together, has taken up residence inside ordinary people. Paul, who once kept the law flawlessly and counted every observance as gain on his ledger, now stakes his entire life on this one fact: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Galatians 2:20). The hope of glory is not a future state you climb toward by effort. It is a present Presence you already carry in your chest. Jesus promised exactly this in the upper room, the night before the cross, to frightened men who would scatter within hours: "If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him" (John 14:23). We will come and live in him. And Paul is now standing in a Gentile world announcing that the promise landed — in pagan cities, in unlikely bodies, the living Christ taking up residence in the very people the religious establishment had already written off as too far gone.

**Stop searching for a deeper thing than Christ**
This is the indictment, and I am standing inside it, because I have wanted more than Christ. Not less. More. I have wanted Christ plus a strategy, Christ plus a feeling I can summon on command, Christ plus the secret the next conference promised to finally hand me — as if the Person who holds the universe together were merely the foundation, and the real building, the thing that would actually satisfy, was something I bolt on top. Paul knew that hunger from the inside and went to war against it on behalf of a church he had never met. He labored, he says, "that their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ; in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:2-3). All of them. Every treasure of wisdom, every treasure of knowledge, hidden — not from you, but for you — in Christ. "Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). There is no deeper room past Him. There is no advanced course beyond Him. There is no inner circle He is not already the center of. Everything the false teachers promised at a price — the wisdom, the fullness, the secret knowledge, the higher tier — is already and entirely inside the One who lives in you. You have been digging for buried treasure in the basement while the treasure was sitting the whole time in your own chest. The mystery the world has hunted across every age was never a thing to be located and decoded. It was a Person who came to live in the people no one expected, and He has a name, and the name is the answer to everything you have been looking for somewhere else.

The mystery has a name.

## Rooted in the One You Already Have
*Stop adding to a Christ who is already complete*

**Text:** Colossians 2:6-23 · **Supporting:** Galatians 3:3 · John 19:30 · Romans 6:4 · Hebrews 10:14

The danger at Colossae was never that they would abandon Christ. It was subtler and far more religious than that. The danger was that they would keep Him and add. Keep Jesus, but add the rules. Keep grace, but add the calendar and the diet and the festival. Keep the cross, but add a little something on top to make it complete — a discipline, a vision, an angelic experience, a special observance, a tier of wisdom the ordinary believer had not yet attained. It looked like devotion. It always looks like devotion. And Paul has one sentence for the whole machine, and it is the most quietly devastating line in the letter.

**You already received Him — so walk in Him**
"As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him: rooted and built up in him, and stablished in the faith, as ye have been taught, abounding therein with thanksgiving" (Colossians 2:6-7). Notice the logic, because the whole argument turns on it. The way you received Him is the way you now walk in Him. You received Him by grace, with empty hands, bringing nothing, adding nothing — so you walk that way too, all the way down, all the way home. The Galatians fell off this exact cliff, and Paul's question to them is the question for every add-on religion since the first century: "Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?" (Galatians 3:3). You started by grace. Why would you finish by effort? Rooted — perfect tense in the Greek, a root already sunk and settled, a thing that happened and stays happened — and being built up, present tense, ongoing, day by ordinary day. The foundation is finished. The construction continues. And you do not re-pour the foundation every time you doubt, every time you sin, every time a teacher tells you the floor you are standing on was never quite enough.

**The fullness is in Him, and you are in the fullness**
Then the hammer comes down. "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power" (Colossians 2:9-10). All the fullness. Not a portion, not an emanation, not a lesser copy. All of it, of the Godhead, bodily, in Christ. And you — already, presently, today, not someday after enough effort — are complete in Him. Filled full in the One who is full. So what exactly were the teachers selling? What do you add to a fullness that is already total? What is the upgrade on everything? The cross said it first, in a single Greek word from a dying mouth: tetelestai — "It is finished" (John 19:30). The word a merchant stamped on a paid invoice. Paid in full. Nothing owing. Hebrews says it just as flat: "by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified" (Hebrews 10:14). Perfected. For ever. By one offering, never to be repeated, never to be supplemented. And Paul drives the legal point all the way home, because the Colossians felt the weight of a debt the rules could never clear: God blotted out "the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross" (Colossians 2:14). The certificate of debt against you, itemized and signed in your own failures, was not refinanced. It was not negotiated down to terms you could manage. It was nailed to the cross and cancelled in His blood. You went under the water with Him and came up alive — "buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God" (Colossians 2:12) — the same death and rising Paul preaches to Rome: "we are buried with him by baptism into death" (Romans 6:4). Dead, buried, raised. What does a raised man add to his own resurrection?

**You are reaching for shadows while holding the substance**
Here is where it has to turn on us, because I know the appeal of the add-on from the inside. The rule feels like rigor. The diet feels like devotion. The special discipline feels like depth, and self-made religion always, always feels more serious than simple trust. Plain dependence on a finished work feels too easy to a soul that wants to contribute. Paul names the whole mechanism without flinching. "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ" (Colossians 2:16-17). A shadow. The festivals, the food laws, the calendar — all of it real once, all of it pointing forward, all of it shadow cast by a body that has now arrived. And you are out there clutching the shadow while the substance Himself is standing in the room. The verdict Paul renders on the entire apparatus is merciless: these things "have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh" (Colossians 2:23). A show of wisdom. The appearance of seriousness. And no power whatsoever against the flesh it claims to master. The rules cannot make you holy. They can only make you proud of how hard you are trying. Every system that adds to Christ is finally an insult to Christ, because under all its earnest discipline it is saying His fullness was not quite enough and His finished work did not quite finish. It did. He is the head, the fullness, the completed offering, and you are already in Him. Stop building a porch onto a finished house. You are not almost complete, one discipline shy. You are complete in Him.

You are complete in Him.

## Set Your Mind Where Your Life Already Is
*Raised with Christ, hidden in God, dressed in the new self*

**Text:** Colossians 3:1-17 · **Supporting:** Romans 6:11 · Galatians 3:27 · Matthew 6:21 · Philippians 4:8

Most moral instruction starts with the command. Do this. Stop that. Try harder, dig deeper, white-knuckle it. Paul will get to commands — he has a long and specific list of what to put off and what to put on — but he flatly refuses to start there. He starts instead with a fact about you, a fact you may not feel and cannot change and did not accomplish. You died. You were raised. And your life is no longer located where you keep looking for it.

**Your life is hidden in a place you cannot reach to ruin it**
"If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God" (Colossians 3:1). Not seek in order to become risen. Seek because you already are. The command rests on an accomplished fact, never the other way around. Then the line that should change the way you breathe. "For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3). Hidden — kekruptai, perfect tense, a completed hiding that still holds today and will hold tomorrow. Your truest life — the real you, the weight of who you are before God — is not in your performance, not in your reputation, not in the fragile thing you spend all day defending and apologizing for and trying to rebuild. It is sealed in God, with Christ, behind a door no threat can open. Paul tells Rome to do the math on this and live off the total: "reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Romans 6:11). Reckon it. Count it as already true, because it is, and you are simply catching your feelings up to the ledger God already closed. So the mind goes up — "set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth" (Colossians 3:2) — for the plainest reason Jesus ever gave about the human heart: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Matthew 6:21). The direction of your attention always, helplessly, follows the location of your treasure. And your treasure is seated at the right hand of God.

**Put off the corpse, put on the man**
Now the commands arrive, and notice they are not self-improvement projects bolted onto a stalled life. They are getting dressed as the person you already are. "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5). Mortify — put to death. You do not manage these things, you do not negotiate a comfortable arrangement with them, you do not contain them. You execute them, because they belong to the corpse you already are in Christ, and a dead man has no business feeding the appetites of a life he has left. "And have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him" (Colossians 3:10). Put on — the same verb Paul hands the Galatians: "For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (Galatians 3:27). You wear Him the way you wear clothing, deliberately, every morning. And the new wardrobe is specific, named garment by garment so you cannot pretend you did not know what to reach for: "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye" (Colossians 3:12-13). Mercy because you were shown mercy. Forgiveness measured by the forgiveness you received at the cross. "And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness" (Colossians 3:14). Love over the whole outfit, like a belt that holds every other garment in place and keeps the rest from falling off.

**You are dressing every morning, and the only question is in what**
Here is the turn, and it lands in the mirror, because I get dressed in the old self more mornings than I will say out loud. I put on the resentment like a familiar coat. I put on the comparison, the scorekeeping, the low-grade contempt for the person who wronged me, and then I call it being honest about how I feel. We do this. We were raised with Christ and we still reach for the grave clothes out of sheer habit, because the corpse is familiar and warm and the new man is not yet comfortable on the shoulders. But Paul will not let the old self be normalized, will not let us treat the old wardrobe as just who we are. The renewal is real and ongoing. The image is genuinely being restored in us. And the marker of the new life Paul names is not strain and effort but a saturated, singing kind of worship: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs... And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him" (Colossians 3:16-17). Whatsoever. Word or deed. All of it carried out under His name. The mind set above naturally feeds on the things Paul lists to Philippi — "whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report" (Philippians 4:8) — not because thinking lovely thoughts earns anything, but because that is simply what a raised mind grazes on when its treasure is above. And underneath every single command in this chapter is the one fact that does all the lifting: "Christ is all, and in all" (Colossians 3:11). All of it. All of you. All the time, in everyone. You are not climbing toward a heavenly life you have not reached. You already have it, hidden with Christ in God where nothing and no one can touch it. So set your mind there, where you already live, and get dressed accordingly.

Set your mind above.

## The Lord of the Whole House
*The supremacy of Christ reaches the kitchen, the workshop, and the prayer closet*

**Text:** Colossians 3:18-4:18 · **Supporting:** Ephesians 6:7 · 1 Corinthians 10:31 · Romans 12:12 · Matthew 5:16

We will follow Christ into the sanctuary. We will follow Him into the dramatic decision, the public stand, the big repentance with witnesses. The harder question — the one this whole letter has been building toward and finally lands on — is whether He is Lord of the Tuesday. The marriage no one applauds. The job no one sees. The dishes, the diapers, the difficult coworker, the hour of work that earns no notice and changes no headline. Paul has spent two chapters on the supremacy of Christ over thrones and dominions and the cohesion of the cosmos. Now he walks that same supremacy straight through the front door of your house.

**The cosmic Lord rules the dinner table**
Watch how one phrase keeps landing, over and over, in every relationship he touches. "Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them. Children, obey your parents in all things: for this is well pleasing unto the Lord" (Colossians 3:18-20). In the Lord. Well pleasing unto the Lord. Not because a household chain of command is sacred in itself, and not because Paul is baptizing the social order of Rome — but because the Christ who holds all things together is now the One every relationship is rendered to. The husband answers to Him. The wife answers to Him. The child, the parent, all of it bends toward the same Lord. And then comes the verse that detonates the whole worldly map of who matters and whose work counts: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Colossians 3:23). He is speaking to slaves when he says it — to the people Rome counted as property, as living tools, as nobody — and he tells them their ordinary forced labor is worship rendered directly to Christ Himself. "With good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men" (Ephesians 6:7). The lowest worker in the entire empire is told that his unseen, uncredited work has a divine audience of One who misses nothing. That single sentence has done more to dignify human labor than every revolution that has marched since. "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31). All of it. The whole unglamorous, unwatched day, lifted up and made holy.

**The supremacy that holds galaxies sustains a prayer life**
Then Paul turns from the household to the closet, and the same Lordship that organizes your labor now organizes your prayer. "Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving" (Colossians 4:2). Continue — proskartereō, to persist, to hold fast, to refuse to quit when nothing seems to be happening and the heavens feel like brass. Watchful and thankful — the two things our prayer almost never is, because we drift off and we grumble. He gives Rome the same charge: "Continuing instant in prayer" (Romans 12:12). And the witness toward the people outside the household of faith is just as ordinary and just as deliberate, no program required: "Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time. Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man" (Colossians 4:5-6). Not a campaign. Not a script memorized for a stranger. A way of speaking to the neighbor over the fence, the coworker at the next desk, the cashier you will never see again — words with grace in them and salt in them, ready for the question when it comes. A life that simply gives off light the way Jesus said it would: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven" (Matthew 5:16).

**He signs off with a list of names, and the names are the whole point**
Here is the turn, and it is gentle, and it quietly implicates every one of us who secretly believes the gospel runs on heroes. I have wanted my ministry to be a stage, and Christ keeps insisting on making it a household — the unseen faithfulness, the people whose names no one will remember, the work rendered to Him and to no audience at all. We want significance. We want our name on the thing. And Paul ends the single most cosmic letter in the New Testament — the letter about the One in whom all things hold together — with a long, plain roll call of ordinary coworkers. Tychicus, the courier. Onesimus, "a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you" (Colossians 4:9) — a runaway slave, named without embarrassment as family. Epaphras, the man who planted Colossae, who is "always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God" (Colossians 4:12). Luke the physician. And even Mark — the man who once quit the mission and walked away — folded back in, restored, useful again. And a single line for a woman hosting a church in her front room: "Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house" (Colossians 4:15). The Christ who holds all things together is carried forth, in the end, not by the famous but by a list of real people who carried the gospel into real houses on real Tuesdays. The supremacy of Christ does not float somewhere above your ordinary life, untouchable and abstract. It comes down — into the marriage, into the workshop, into the prayer you almost stopped praying, into the name no one outside your kitchen will ever remember — and it makes every inch of it worship. There is no part of your ordinary day He is not Lord of. There is no labor too small, no name too obscure, to be rendered straight to Him. So whatever is in front of you right now, the dishes or the deal or the difficult person, do it for Him.

Whatever you do, do it for Him.
